patterns.role_note: 2010: Independent Victims' Protection Commission (Klasnic Commission), set up by bishops spring 2010. Set a four-tier compensation model (EUR 5,000 / 15,000 / 25,000 / more in extreme cases)

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Wilhelminenberg children's home, Vienna — commission report; Tyrol and Vorarlberg — state-commissioned study of welfare and residential care (2015); Tyrol — 'Dreierkommission Martinsbühel' report on church-run children's homes (2022); Vienna — historians' commission (2012) and Weisser Ring support programme for victims of city youth welfare (2010–2019).

cases.title: Bergisch Gladbach abuse complex
cases.who: Chat groups of men sharing recordings of abuse of their own and other children
cases.what: In October 2019 police found a large cache of child abuse images and videos at a house in Bergisch Gladbach; the man there had repeatedly abused his daughter, born in 2017, and shared recordings in chat groups. On 6 October 2020 Cologne Regional Court sentenced him to 12 years plus preventive detention. Investigators found more than 30,000 pseudonyms used in the network, many untraceable; by January 2022 Cologne police had identified 439 suspects, secured numerous convictions and rescued 65 children aged from three months to 17. Two other men, from Krefeld and Viersen, were sentenced to 14.5 and 13.5 years.

cases.title: Elysium darknet platform
cases.who: Elysium (darknet forum and chats, over 87,000 members)
cases.what: Elysium existed from late 2016 and was used to exchange abuse material and to arrange the sexual abuse of children; it had German, French, Spanish and Italian chat groups. German prosecutors (ZIT Frankfurt) and the BKA shut it down in June 2017 after Australian police passed on a lead; 14 suspects were arrested, 12 suspected of abusing children themselves. On 7 March 2019 the Limburg court sentenced four men to between 3 years 10 months and 9 years 9 months, with preventive detention for the main administrator.

cases.title: Wilhelminenberg children's home, Vienna — commission report
cases.who: City of Vienna children's home at Wilhelminenberg
cases.what: A commission set up by the City of Vienna presented a 344-page report on 12 June 2013, based on 217 interviews including 140 former residents. It found children at the city-run home (1948–1977, girls only from 1962) were rampantly abused, including rape and sexual exploitation by caregivers and outside men, with girls as young as about six. Findings were sent to prosecutors. Some former residents received payments of up to €35,000.
cases.cover_up: Municipal staff in the overseeing department knew of widespread abuse and did not act; city politicians who learned of it in the 1960s also ignored it.

cases.title: Tyrol and Vorarlberg — state-commissioned study of welfare and residential care (2015)
cases.who: State welfare system and residential homes of Tyrol and Vorarlberg, incl. Jagdberg (Schlins), St. Martin (Schwaz), Mariatal (Kramsach), Kleinvolderberg
cases.what: A University of Innsbruck team led by Michaela Ralser, commissioned by the state governments of Tyrol and Vorarlberg, presented its overall study of welfare and residential care on 6 July 2015. It examined four state institutions in detail (Jagdberg, St. Martin, Mariatal and Kleinvolderberg) and found a total institution of isolation and dependence that produced, tolerated and did not prevent physical, psychological and sexualised violence until the 1980s. By then 362 people in Tyrol and 159 in Vorarlberg had received compensation from the states since 2010.
cases.cover_up: The study found the institutional system produced, tolerated and failed to prevent physical, psychological and sexualised violence.

cases.title: Tyrol — 'Dreierkommission Martinsbühel' report on church-run children's homes (2022)
cases.who: Seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol (Martinsbühel, Scharnitz, Josefinum/Volders, Bubenburg/Fügen, St. Josef/Mils, Thurnfeld/Hall, Elisabethinum/Axams); Diocese of Innsbruck; Tyrolean youth welfare
cases.what: A commission set up in 2019 by the State of Tyrol, the Diocese of Innsbruck and religious orders, chaired by Margret Aull, presented its final report 'Demut lernen' on 7 December 2022, written by historians Ina Friedmann and Friedrich Stepanek. Based on 75 interviews, it covered seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol after 1945, where former residents described structural, physical, psychological and sexualised violence; at Martinsbühel in the 1970s one sister looked after up to 50 girls. Survivors said state youth welfare and school authorities did not look closely enough. Bishop Hermann Glettler called the findings 'total pedagogical failure' in church and state institutions, and the state social affairs councillor apologised.
cases.cover_up: Survivors said the state youth welfare office and school authorities looked too little; church and state officials acknowledged institutional responsibility.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Vienna — historians' commission (2012) and Weisser Ring support programme for victims of city youth welfare (2010–2019)
cases.who: City of Vienna youth welfare — municipal, church and private children's homes and foster care, incl. the Kinderübernahmestelle (KÜST)
cases.what: A historians' commission led by Reinhard Sieder reported in May 2012 on Vienna's municipal, church and private children's homes after 1945, through which roughly 100,000 children passed; it described sadistic sexual abuse by some staff alongside widespread violence. The City of Vienna commissioned the victim-support organisation Weisser Ring in 2010 to handle claims of people harmed in Vienna youth welfare institutions between 1945 and 1999. Its final report (2019) records 3,139 reports and financial aid to 2,384 people, with 42.13 million euros paid directly to victims. The separate Wilhelminenberg commission is already on the map.

cases.title: SOS-Kinderdorf Austria — abuse at Imst and Moosburg, founder Hermann Gmeiner, and the Griss reform commission (2025–2026)
cases.who: SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich — children's villages incl. Imst (Tyrol) and Moosburg (Carinthia); founder Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986)
cases.what: After a Falter report in September 2025 on abuse by staff at Austrian SOS children's villages, SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich said on 23 October 2025 that there were credible allegations that its founder Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986) sexually and physically abused eight boys at four villages between the 1950s and 1980s; victims had come forward from 2013 and received compensation and therapy, but the organisation had not made this public. A later investigation report listed 16 suspected cases of sexualised violence by Gmeiner. An external reform commission chaired by former Supreme Court president Irmgard Griss presented its results on 25 June 2026, focusing on abuse at Moosburg and Imst, handling of earlier studies and possible cover-ups, and the lack of external oversight. Prosecutors in Klagenfurt, Innsbruck and Salzburg opened investigations.
cases.cover_up: The allegations against Gmeiner were known internally for years (victims came forward 2013–2023) but were made public only in 2025.

cases.title: Cardinal Groër affair and Klasnic victims' commission, Austria
cases.who: Archdiocese of Vienna; Austrian Bishops' Conference; Independent Victims' Protection Commission (Klasnic Commission)
cases.what: Archbishop of Vienna Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër stepped down in September 1995 after a former pupil, followed by others, accused him of sexual abuse; in 1998 Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded, and the Holy See opened an inquiry. In spring 2010 the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission chaired by Waltraud Klasnic. By 31 August 2021, according to the church's victims' foundation, payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total. At Kremsmünster Abbey, the former head of the boarding school was jailed for 12 years in 2013 for crimes against 24 former pupils, 15 of them victims of sexual abuse.

cases.title: New Zealand DIA-led operation: 146 children safeguarded
cases.who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
cases.what: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. By March 2022 it had opened 836 cases internationally, led to 46 arrests across New Zealand, identified more than 100 suspects in the EU and safeguarded 146 children; in Austria and Hungary suspects were abusing their own children.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Austria-led 2007 investigation — 2,360 suspects in 77 countries
cases.who: Online distribution network uncovered by Austrian authorities
cases.what: The investigation began in July 2006 when an employee of a Vienna-based file-hosting service reported suspicious material; within 24 hours investigators recorded more than 8,000 hits from 2,361 IP addresses in 77 countries. On 7 February 2007 Austrian authorities announced more than 2,360 suspects who had paid to view videos of young children being sexually abused; the FBI was investigating about 600, about 130 were Australian, France was looking at about 100 and at least 23 were Austrian. Germany had the largest number of suspects. No suspects were yet in custody at the announcement.
cases.cover_up: The two Irish suspects were not investigated by the Garda until six months after Austria notified them.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

cases.title: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.

networks.name: Elysium
networks.what: Darknet forum with over 87,000 members used to share material and arrange abuse; four operators convicted 2019.

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: North Rhine-Westphalia abuse complexes (Lügde, Bergisch Gladbach)
networks.what: Linked series of investigations into men abusing children and sharing recordings in chat groups; Bergisch Gladbach alone produced 439 suspects. Münster complex (2020) not documented here — page not retrieved.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors.
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Proven link to a state service
patterns.role_note: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors (proven link to a state service).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

cases.title: Bosnia — Foča rape camps; ICTY Kunarac judgment (girls as young as 12 enslaved)
cases.who: Bosnian Serb army (VRS) and paramilitaries; local police chief named in testimony
cases.what: In Serb-held Foča in 1992–93, Bosniak women and girls were held at detention sites such as Partizan Sports Hall, next to the municipal police building, and taken from there to apartments and private houses to be raped; the ICTY found rape was used by Bosnian Serb forces as an instrument of terror and that local police guarded the women and joined in their mistreatment. On 22 February 2001 the ICTY sentenced Dragoljub Kunarac, a VRS reconnaissance unit leader, to 28 years for torture, rape and enslavement; Radomir Kovač to 20 years for enslavement, rape and outrages upon personal dignity, including detaining two girls in his apartment for about four months and selling victims to other soldiers; and Zoran Vuković to 12 years for torture and rape, including raping a girl he knew to be 15. The sentences were upheld on appeal on 12 June 2002.

cases.title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.

flows.title: Moldova/Romania/Ukraine → Bosnia: trafficking of women and girls
flows.what: Women and girls mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine sold to Bosnian bar owners; local police, IPTF monitors and US contractors implicated.

networks.name: Lev Tahor
networks.what: Ultra-Orthodox sect of about 200–300 people founded in Israel in 1988 by Shlomo Helbrans, accused of child abuse and forced marriage of teenage girls. Leaders were convicted in the US in 2021 of kidnapping two children.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Chile → Peru: Marist Brother Abel Pérez; Germany → South America: Jesuit Fr Wolfgang S..
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Colonia Dignidad (Paul Schäfer): first report 1967, first action 1996 (29 years). Escapees' allegations in the 1960s (Wolfgang Müller; Heinz Kuhn 1967) were rejected by politicians because of the colony's ties to those preparing the 1973 coup; colony served as a DINA torture centre Fernando Karadima: first report 1984, first action 2011 (27 years). Parishioners reported him to Archbishop Fresno in 1984; a credible church investigation (2004-05) was shelved by Cardinal Errázuriz
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Paul Schäfer / Colonia Dignidad: Hopp living in Germany; investigation dropped
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2019: Chile — Chamber of Deputies commission on irregular adoptions (2019)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Proven link to a state service
patterns.role_note: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site (proven link to a state service). Colonia Dignidad — Paul Schäfer convicted of abusing 25 children (proven link to a state service).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–); SENAME — deaths and abuse in Chilean state child protection; Chile — 'Informe Jeldres' (Judiciary/UNICEF audit of residential care homes); Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site; Chile — Chamber of Deputies commission on irregular adoptions (2019); Colonia Dignidad — Paul Schäfer convicted of abusing 25 children.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site
cases.who: Colonia Dignidad sect led by Paul Schäfer; Chile's secret police DINA; West German embassy
cases.what: Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal wanted in Germany on child abuse charges, founded the Colonia Dignidad commune in southern Chile in 1961. Chilean officials believe the colony was used as a centre for torture of opponents of the Pinochet dictatorship between 1973 and 1990, and Schäfer was charged with aiding the regime. The colony recruited children from local farms into its free school and clinic; an investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer fled to Argentina, was arrested there in March 2005 and returned to Chile, and on 24–25 May 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children; with further convictions for torture, weapons and a murder his sentences totalled 33 years. He died in prison in 2010. The colony's doctor, Hartmut Hopp, was convicted in Chile in 2011 of 16 counts of aiding child sexual abuse.
cases.cover_up: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them. Schäfer fled in 1997 and was caught in Argentina in March 2005.

cases.title: Spiniak case, Chile — child exploitation ring and false accusation against a senator
cases.who: Claudio Spiniak (businessman)
cases.what: Businessman Claudio Spiniak was arrested in 2003 accused of leading a network that sexually abused and exploited adolescents. In 2008 Chile's Supreme Court sentenced him to 12 years for sexual abuse of minors, promoting their exploitation and producing pornographic material; he was released in 2013 and died in March 2026. A witness claimed that members of Congress attended his parties — claims publicly backed by a deputy and a former priest — but she later admitted she had lied; the politicians named were cleared (proceedings dismissed for lack of evidence). The political-network claim is disproved.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
cases.who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
cases.what: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.

cases.title: Chile — National Prosecutor's Office: 166 investigations of clergy and church workers, 248 victims (2019)
cases.who: Catholic clergy, religious and lay church workers; 152 priests, 10 bishops, 9 deacons, 15 lay people and 27 non-clerical members of orders among those investigated
cases.what: Chile's National Prosecutor's Office reviewed sexual abuse by members of the Catholic Church nationally. Its balance of 30 April 2019 counted 166 investigations and 221 people investigated (152 priests, 10 bishops, 9 deacons, 15 lay people and 27 non-clerical members of orders), and 248 victims, of whom 131 were children or adolescents, 35 adults and 82 not recorded. In July 2018 the office had already reported five cases of alleged cover-up or obstruction aimed at bishops or superiors of congregations.

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: SENAME — deaths and abuse in Chilean state child protection
cases.who: Servicio Nacional de Menores (SENAME), Ministry of Justice, and accredited private residences
cases.what: The death of an 11-year-old girl at SENAME's Galvarino centre in Santiago in April 2016 exposed conditions in the system; in October 2016 SENAME disclosed 1,313 deaths of people in its programmes between 2005 and mid-2016. In a report released on 30 July 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the Chilean state responsible for 'grave violations' of the Convention, including sexual abuse, torture and cruel treatment in SENAME residences over 40 years, overcrowding of up to 60% and 210 deaths in residences 2005–2016. A former national director was questioned as a suspect over children's deaths in 2018.

cases.title: Chile — 'Informe Jeldres' (Judiciary/UNICEF audit of residential care homes)
cases.who: SENAME-accredited residential care homes (hogares), run by private organisations under state supervision
cases.what: Family-court judges led by Judge Mónica Jeldres, with UNICEF, interviewed children in residential homes between July and November 2012. The report found sexual abuse was a constant in the homes and that 10% of children in state protection had been involved in some form of sexual abuse as victim or perpetrator. In one Arica home it found a sexual exploitation network organised by carers: 24 girls left the home and returned drugged at dawn. After publication the government ordered 34 homes intervened, SENAME closed four residences, the prosecutor's office opened investigations and deputies announced a congressional investigating commission.
cases.cover_up: The report was delivered to the Judiciary in March 2013 but held back over methodological criticism until CIPER published it in July 2013; legislators said the Justice Minister had known since March.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Chile — Chamber of Deputies commission on irregular adoptions (2019)
cases.who: Hospital medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff, private intermediary organisations
cases.what: A special investigating commission of the Chamber of Deputies, chaired by Deputy Boris Barrera, worked from January to 22 July 2019 on children taken from mainly poor, often rural mothers, some of whom were made to believe their babies had died, and given for adoption, many abroad, before, during and after the 1973–1990 dictatorship. It found complicity by medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff and organisations operating outside hospitals, and noted that private intermediaries were paid for their role. It recommended an international DNA bank, a national truth commission on irregular adoptions and excluding private bodies from adoption; the Chamber approved the report on 4 October 2019 by 88 votes with 13 abstentions.
cases.cover_up: Some hospitals did not register or destroyed birth records from 1970 onward (e.g. Carlos Van Buren hospital, Valparaíso); the commission also found gaps in birth and departure records

cases.title: Fernando Karadima, Bishop Barros and Chile's bishops' resignation offer
cases.who: Archdiocese of Santiago; Fr Fernando Karadima; Bishop Juan Barros; Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati
cases.what: The Vatican found Fr Fernando Karadima guilty of sexual abuse in 2011 and sentenced him to a life of prayer and penance; Pope Francis dismissed him from the priesthood on 27 September 2018, announced the next day. Four of his protégés became bishops, including Juan Barros of Osorno, whom Francis had defended. After receiving a 2,300-page report from Archbishop Charles Scicluna, Francis wrote in April 2018 that he had been mistaken in his assessment of the situation in Chile. Every bishop in Chile offered to resign in May 2018; by the end of June five resignations, including Barros's (11 June), had been accepted. In October 2018 an appeals court found the Archdiocese of Santiago liable for covering up for Karadima in a suit by three survivors naming Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati.
cases.cover_up: Parishioners reported Karadima to Archbishop Fresno in 1984; Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a credible 2004–05 investigation; Barros, a Karadima protégé, made bishop of Osorno in 2015

cases.title: Marist Brothers Chile — Brother Abel Pérez
cases.who: Marist Brothers in Chile
cases.what: In 2017 the Chilean Marist Brothers acknowledged that Brother Abel Pérez abused at least 14 minors between the 1970s and 2000. He had confessed to superiors in 2010 and was then transferred to Peru. Police investigated complaints at many of the order's schools.
cases.cover_up: After confessing to superiors in 2010, Pérez was transferred to Peru

cases.title: Pope Francis' letter to Chile's bishops and the Scicluna mission (2018)
cases.who: Pope Francis; Archbishop Charles Scicluna; Mgr Jordi Bertomeu
cases.what: After defending Bishop Juan Barros in January 2018, Pope Francis sent Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, who took 64 depositions in New York and Santiago; their report ran to more than 2,300 pages. In a letter of 8 April 2018 Francis wrote that he had 'made serious errors in the assessment and perception of the situation, in particular through the lack of reliable and balanced information', and summoned the Chilean bishops to Rome, where all of them offered to resign in May 2018.

cases.title: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad
cases.who: German Foreign Office; Colonia Dignidad
cases.what: In April 2016 Germany released Foreign Office files from 1986–1996 and the foreign minister admitted diplomats had failed colony residents, including abused children. In 2017 the Bundestag formally acknowledged German responsibility and asked the government to plan an investigation, memorial and help for victims; in 2019 Germany announced compensation payments to victims.
cases.cover_up: Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said in April 2016 that 'over the course of many years, from the 60s to the 80s, German diplomats at best looked away' and that the embassy failed to shield Germans at the colony.

flows.what: Charged with child abuse in Chile, Schäfer disappeared on 20 May 1997 and hid in Argentina until found in a gated community in Tortuguitas in March 2005 and returned to Chile.

flows.what: Colony doctor Hartmut Hopp, under house arrest awaiting trial, fled Chile for Germany in May 2011. German prosecutors sought in 2016 to enforce a five-year sentence imposed in Chile, then dropped their own investigation in May 2019.

networks.name: Colonia Dignidad / Villa Baviera
networks.what: German sect enclave in Chile led by Paul Schäfer, convicted in 2006 of abusing 25 minors. Used by Pinochet's secret police DINA as a detention and torture site (Rettig Commission 1991). Germany's president acknowledged diplomatic failures in 2016.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

networks.name: Society of Jesus (Jesuits)
networks.what: The 2010 Canisius-Kolleg disclosures in Berlin started Germany's abuse reckoning. In 2023 El País published the diary of Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas recording abuse of more than 80 minors in Bolivia, with superiors aware from 1978.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Costa Rica → Mexico: Fr Mauricio Víquez (flight, extradited 2021).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

cases.title: Costa Rica — Fr Mauricio Víquez, convicted after fleeing to Mexico
cases.who: Archdiocese of San José; Episcopal Conference of Costa Rica
cases.what: Víquez, a former church spokesman on family issues, fled Costa Rica in 2018 when accusations surfaced, going via Panama to San Nicolás de los Garza, Mexico, where he was caught; he was extradited in 2021. In August 2022 a civil court ordered the archbishop and two church entities to pay about US$100,000 in damages.
cases.cover_up: A San José civil court ordered Archbishop José Rafael Quirós, the Episcopal Conference and the church's property entity to pay 65 million colones; the victims' lawyer said the church knew from 2002 and did nothing. Three other complaints were declared time-barred.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found Middle East and North Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.
