patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2019: Myanmar — UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission (2018–2019).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Myanmar — Tatmadaw sexual violence against Rohingya and ethnic minority women, girls and boys (UN FFM). Myanmar — abduction of children by armed forces and armed groups (UN verified).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

cases.who: Myanmar armed forces and Pyu Saw Htee; KIA; MNDAA; PDFs
cases.what: The UN verified the abduction of 85 children in Myanmar in 2024, 41 by the Myanmar armed forces and affiliated militias and 33 by the KIA, mostly for recruitment; it verified the rape of 2 girls (Myanmar armed forces 1, KIA 1).

cases.who: Myanmar armed forces (Tatmadaw)
cases.what: The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar found in 2018 that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped during the 2017 'clearance operations', 80% of corroborated cases being gang rapes, and its August 2019 report found sexual and gender-based violence a 'hallmark' of Tatmadaw operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan. cases.title: Myanmar — Pathein monastery: four schoolgirls raped
cases.who: Saitta Thuka monastery (Theravada Buddhist monastic boarding)
cases.what: Four girls aged 10 to 14 staying free at a monastery so they could attend school were repeatedly raped from June 2017 by the monastery's administrator monk, according to the children and families interviewed by Myanmar Now. The abuse came to light in February 2018; police issued orders to arrest him on sight across several regions. TIME reported up to 300,000 children may live in Myanmar monasteries, with few records kept.
cases.cover_up: The monk disappeared when parents went to police; TIME found police unable or unwilling to say whether a search continued, and described near-blanket immunity for monks, with police deferring to the religious affairs ministry and the Sangha. An ex-monk who reprimanded him was told to move away.

cases.title: Myanmar → China — Kachin women and girls sold as 'brides' (HRW 2019)
cases.who: Traffickers including relatives and acquaintances; buying families in China
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's 112-page report of 21 March 2019 documented women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States, many displaced by conflict, sold for US$3,000–13,000 to Chinese families, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. One survivor was trafficked at 16 by her sister-in-law. The 2025 US TIP report says displaced women and girls in Kachin and Shan remain vulnerable to forced marriage and forced childbearing in China.
cases.cover_up: HRW said Myanmar and Chinese authorities were 'looking away'; police on both sides gave traffickers little reason to fear enforcement.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2021: suspension: Netherlands suspends all intercountry adoption with immediate effect after Joustra committee report (8 February) 2024: ban: Netherlands announces citizens will no longer be allowed to adopt from abroad (May)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2013: Terre des Hommes "Sweetie" sting: 20,000 internet users in 10 weeks offered to pay for webcam sex with an apparent Filipino child; of 21,000 perpetrators, 1,000 were identified (from Australia, Canada, Germany, India, the Netherlands, the UK, the US and others), incl. 110 in the UK and 254 in the US — early evidence of "webcam child sex tourism"
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 33,788 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (11% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Amsterdam daycare abuse case (Het Hofnarretje) and the Gunning commission
cases.who: Robert Mikelsons (childcare worker at Het Hofnarretje and Jenno's Knuffelparadijs) and his partner Richard van O.
cases.what: Childcare worker Robert Mikelsons abused babies and toddlers at two Amsterdam daycare centres and as a babysitter between February 2007 and January 2010. On 21 May 2012 the Amsterdam district court sentenced him to 18 years plus compulsory psychiatric detention (TBS); he was charged over 67 children and admitted abusing 87, and the appeal court raised the sentence to 19 years on 26 April 2013. His partner Richard van O. was sentenced to six years as an accessory. On 15 April 2011 a commission chaired by Louise Gunning-Schepers found that daycare centres, government bodies and others had failed, that risk signals were missed, and that a 2008 anonymous report had not been acted on.
cases.cover_up: An anonymous tip to Meld Misdaad Anoniem in 2008 was not acted on; the Gunning commission called it a missed opportunity.

cases.title: Special Court for Sierra Leone — Charles Taylor convicted of aiding sexual slavery and use of child soldiers (2012)
cases.who: Charles Taylor, former President of Liberia; Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and allied rebel forces he aided
cases.what: On 26 April 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone, sitting in The Hague, convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor on all 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, on the basis of aiding and abetting crimes by the Revolutionary United Front during Sierra Leone's civil war, including sexual slavery and the recruitment and use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years in prison in May 2012.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Operation Torpedo — FBI ran three Tor sites
cases.who: Three Tor-hidden abuse sites run by a Nebraska man
cases.what: Dutch police compromised one site and found it physically hosted at a Nebraska web host; the FBI found an employee running two sites at work and one at home. After a year of surveillance the FBI arrested him and operated the sites for two weeks, using a network investigative technique to reveal visitors' IP addresses. The US DOJ said in December 2015 that 18 US users had been convicted besides the operator; one was the acting cybersecurity director of the US Department of Health and Human Services.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: Peter Scully — pay-per-view abuse streamed from Mindanao
cases.who: 'No Limits Fun' dark web site (Peter Scully, Australian; Filipino accomplices)
cases.what: An Australian from Melbourne who moved to Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, in 2011 was alleged to have run a ring that abused children and sold videos of the abuse online to customers abroad. The Philippine investigation began with a tip from Dutch police, who found images on a seized hard drive. Arrested in 2015, he was charged with the murder of a 12-year-old girl as well as trafficking and child abuse. In June 2018 a Cagayan de Oro court sentenced him to life imprisonment after convicting him of one count of human trafficking and five counts of rape. On 3 November 2022, under a plea bargain, he was sentenced to a further 129 years; his former girlfriend, a co-accused, got 126 years and two others more than nine years each.

cases.title: Netherlands — National Rapporteur estimate of exploited Dutch girls
cases.who: Domestic pimps and 'loverboy' recruiters
cases.what: A report by National Rapporteur Corinne Dettmeijer, prepared with UNODC and published 18 October 2017, estimated that at least 1,320 underage Dutch girls aged 12 to 17 fall victim to sexual exploitation in the Netherlands each year, using 2012–2016 data. Underage girls made up nearly half of female victims in the Dutch sex industry. In October 2025 the current rapporteur reported reported exploitation cases rising from 868 (2023) to 944 (2024), with more teenage victims.

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: Samson Commission — sexual abuse of children in Dutch state care
cases.who: Dutch children's homes and foster care (Jeugdzorg)
cases.what: The commission chaired by former procurator-general Rieke Samson reported in October 2012 on sexual abuse of children in state-arranged care since 1945. It received 800 claims, 65% about children's homes and 30% about foster families, and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor. It found the government, care homes and foster care services did not do enough to protect children and, once aware, lacked professionalism and courage to act.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: De Winter Commission — violence in Dutch youth care since 1945
cases.who: Dutch residential youth care, foster care, juvenile justice institutions, closed youth care, shelters for unaccompanied asylum-seeking minors, institutions for disabled children
cases.what: The commission led by Professor Micha de Winter published 'Onvoldoende beschermd' on 14 June 2019 after interviewing about 1,000 people who had lived in foster families or youth institutions. It found that a considerable share of children in Dutch youth care since 1945 were not adequately protected from physical, psychological and sexual violence, that supervisors did not intervene enough, and that the government did too little to prevent it. The cabinet said the violence 'should never have happened' and set up a payment scheme for victims.

cases.title: Netherlands — De Vries Commission on sexual abuse in organised sport (2017)
cases.who: Dutch sports clubs and federations; NOC*NSF
cases.what: The Dutch Olympic Committee NOC*NSF set up a commission led by former minister Klaas de Vries in May 2017; it reported on 12 December 2017. A survey found about 12% of athletes had experienced sexually transgressive behaviour as children and about 4% sexual assault or rape. The commission analysed 686 cases reported between 2001 and 2017, in which 60% of victims were under 16 and 70% of perpetrators were coaches or supervisors, and received 103 new reports. It recommended a reporting duty for sports boards.

cases.title: Deetman Commission — supplementary inquiry into abuse of and violence against girls in the Catholic Church (2013)
cases.who: Roman Catholic Church in the Netherlands — dioceses and religious orders
cases.what: The Deetman Commission presented a supplementary inquiry on 11 March 2013 into sexual abuse of and violence against girls and young women who were minors in the Dutch Catholic Church from 1945 to 2012, after its 2011 report had found over 77% of identified victims were male. It received 79 new reports, of which 37 concerned only physical or psychological violence, and reconsidered 71 earlier reports of violence, 26 from women. It called on bishops and religious superiors to reach out to these victims; reports involving sexual abuse go to the Church's reporting point and compensation committees.

cases.title: Deetman Commission — Catholic Church in the Netherlands
cases.who: Catholic dioceses and religious orders in the Netherlands
cases.what: The commission led by former minister Wim Deetman, set up by the church in March 2010, reported on 16 December 2011. It identified at least 800 priests, monks and other religious who abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated tens of thousands of victims. It found bishops and officials knew of the abuse and followed a policy of avoiding scandal.
cases.cover_up: Policy of 'not hanging out the dirty washing'; bishops and officials knew and did not act

cases.title: Utrecht University / WODC study — Jehovah's Witnesses in the Netherlands
cases.who: Jehovah's Witnesses (Netherlands)
cases.what: A study by Utrecht University researchers led by Kees van den Bos, commissioned by the Ministry of Justice's research centre WODC, was published on 23 January 2020. 751 participants reported experiences; only 27% of cases led to a police report. Victims were critical of internal handling by elders; the researchers recommended better support, elder training, an internal reporting centre, and that lawmakers consider a duty to report abuse to police.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Europol: at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children missing in Europe (2016)
cases.who: Europol; organized crime exploiting the migrant flow
cases.what: On 31 January 2016 Europol's chief of staff Brian Donald told The Observer that at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy and 1,000 in Sweden, and that Europol had evidence some had been sexually exploited. He said an entire criminal infrastructure had developed over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow, with many arrests in Germany and Hungary. Save the Children estimated 26,000 unaccompanied children arrived in 2015.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
cases.who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
cases.what: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.

cases.title: Operation Atlas — Virtual Global Taskforce P2P sweep
cases.who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
cases.what: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.

cases.title: Project COMPASS against 'The Com' network
cases.who: The Com (decentralised online network incl. 764, CVLT)
cases.what: Coordinated by Europol's European Counter Terrorism Centre with EU states, Norway, Switzerland, the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand (28 countries). Since January 2025 it has contributed to 30 arrests, 179 identified or partially identified perpetrators, 62 identified or partially identified victims and 4 victims safeguarded. The FBI warned the public about The Com on 23 July 2025.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

flows.title: Seoul → Netherlands
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Netherlands; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Colombo → Netherlands
flows.what: Sri Lankan babies adopted to the Netherlands in the 1980s, many through baby farms and falsified papers; others went to the UK, Sweden, Denmark and Germany.

flows.title: Athens → Netherlands
flows.what: Greek-born children adopted to Netherlands 1950–1975; Greece restored their citizenship by law on 2 May 2025.

flows.title: Buyers in 24 countries → Philippines (HSI data)
flows.what: Europol's 2024 sprint on US HSI data: chats between about 12,000 criminal customer accounts and 100 sellers in the Philippines; packages may lead 24 countries to 197 buyers. Origin point is The Hague (sprint host), not a buyer country.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in the Netherlands (IWF 2025)
flows.what: The Netherlands was the largest host of IWF-actioned material for years (47% in 2018); its share fell to 11% in 2025. INHOPE 2025 still ranks it first for confirmed CSAM (36%).

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Dreamboard
networks.what: Invitation-only board, about 600 members; 72 charged in Operation Delego (2011). Start year is approximate (investigation launched 2009).

networks.name: Boylover forum

networks.name: Boystown
networks.what: Tor platform with 400,000 registered users; four German administrators sentenced 7–12 years (2022).

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Lima → Bolivia: Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas; Chile → Peru: Marist Brother Abel Pérez.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2016: Commission commissioned by Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (report Feb 2017). Founder Luis Figari sexually abused at least one minor and others
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 2,049 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Peru — foreign tourists exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Amazon (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana — suppressed by the Vatican 2025
cases.who: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae; founder Luis Fernando Figari
cases.what: Journalists Pedro Salinas and Paola Ugaz exposed abuse by founder Luis Fernando Figari and associates in the 2015 book 'Mitad monjes, mitad soldados'. An apostolic visitor was appointed in 2015. In February 2017 the group gave Peruvian prosecutors information from an expert report on sexual abuse of minors by Figari and four former members, and the Vatican barred Figari from contact with members. After an investigation by Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, the Vatican expelled Figari in August 2024 over physical, psychological and sexual violence, including against minors. The society was formally suppressed by a decree signed on 14 April 2025.
cases.cover_up: Abuse reported by journalists in 2015 after years of internal silence; journalists faced legal action; Vatican commission in 2023 led to mass expulsions

cases.title: Marist Brothers Chile — Brother Abel Pérez
cases.who: Marist Brothers in Chile
cases.what: In 2017 the Chilean Marist Brothers acknowledged that Brother Abel Pérez abused at least 14 minors between the 1970s and 2000. He had confessed to superiors in 2010 and was then transferred to Peru. Police investigated complaints at many of the order's schools.
cases.cover_up: After confessing to superiors in 2010, Pérez was transferred to Peru

cases.title: La Pampa, Madre de Dios — Operación Mercurio 2019 and sex trafficking in mining camps
cases.who: Bar/brothel networks serving illegal gold-mining camps
cases.what: On 19–20 February 2019 more than 1,500 military and police began Operación Mercurio against illegal gold mining in La Pampa, in the Tambopata reserve buffer zone, under a state of emergency. Peru's Women's Minister said the worst crimes, including child sexual exploitation and child labour, had been committed there, and her ministry took in minors and women rescued from trafficking. Reporting in 2022 said police were still dismantling networks recruiting women to La Pampa bars; a 16-year-old girl previously rescued from a La Pampa trafficking band was found murdered at km 108 in April 2021.

cases.title: Peru — foreign tourists exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Amazon (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Criminal groups transporting tourists on the Amazon
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says tourists from the US and Europe exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Peruvian Amazon, and in Loreto criminal groups take foreign tourists by boat to remote venues on the Amazon River where women and children are exploited. Peruvian, Venezuelan and Bolivian women and girls are lured to mining and logging camps. Courts convicted 59 traffickers in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Authorities charged two police officers for crimes against trafficking victims; corruption remained a significant concern.

flows.title: Cúcuta → Ecuador, Peru, Argentina (Tren de Aragua transfers)
flows.what: Tren de Aragua reportedly used Cúcuta's transport hub to move trafficking victims to Argentina, Ecuador and Peru.

flows.what: After confessing to superiors in 2010 that he had abused minors, Brother Abel Pérez was transferred by the Marist Brothers to Peru.

flows.title: Lima → Bolivia: Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas
flows.what: Spanish Jesuit Pedrajas settled in Bolivia after his first abuse in Lima in 1964, then abused more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools there; he confessed to a superior in 1978, who covered it up.

networks.name: Tren de Aragua
networks.what: Transnational criminal organization originating in Venezuela. US TIP 2025 says it operates sex-trafficking networks in Colombia, using daily-debt lodging (pagadiarios) to control victims, and has affiliated groups in Peru.

networks.what: Lay society founded in Lima in 1971 by Luis Fernando Figari. Exposed by journalists in 2015; investigators found sexual abuse of minors and adults by Figari and others. Figari and over a dozen members were expelled in 2024 and Pope Francis signed its suppression on 14 January 2025.

patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found Middle East and North Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Israel/Gaza — UN COI findings on sexual violence incl. against Palestinian boys and on 7 October
cases.who: Israeli security forces (detention and arrest); Hamas and other armed groups (7 October)
cases.what: The UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel found in June 2024 that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians to sexual and gender-based violence including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, and that 'men and boys were targeted in particular ways'; it found gender persecution of Palestinian men and boys as a crime against humanity. It also found sexual violence was committed on 7 October 2023 at the Nova festival, Nahal Oz and several kibbutzim, and that 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage. Recorded only to the extent of these UN findings.

cases.title: Gulf states block Roblox over child safety (2025)
cases.who: Roblox Corporation
cases.what: In August 2025 Qatar blocked access to Roblox (13 August) and Kuwait's telecoms regulator temporarily blocked it (21 August) after parents and community groups raised child-safety concerns; Turkey had blocked it on 7 August. Roblox had been banned in Oman and Jordan since 2020, and was banned in the UAE from 2018 to 2021. Wikipedia additionally reports that Bahraini MPs drafted a ban, Palestine announced a ban in November 2025, Kazakhstan's and Kyrgyzstan's authorities warned parents about predators, and Buenos Aires and three Argentine provinces blocked it on school devices after grooming reports.

cases.title: Special Court for Sierra Leone — RUF leaders convicted of sexual slavery, forced marriage and use of child soldiers (2009)
cases.who: Revolutionary United Front (RUF): Issa Sesay, Morris Kallon, Augustine Gbao
cases.what: On 25 February 2009 the Special Court for Sierra Leone convicted RUF leaders Issa Sesay and Morris Kallon on 16 of 18 counts and Augustine Gbao on 14. All three were convicted of sexual slavery and of forced marriage as a crime against humanity, the first forced-marriage convictions by an international criminal tribunal; Sesay and Kallon were also convicted of using child soldiers, while Gbao was acquitted of that charge. They were sentenced to 52, 40 and 25 years, and on 26 October 2009 the Appeals Chamber upheld the convictions and sentences, overturning only Gbao's conviction for collective punishments.

cases.title: Special Court for Sierra Leone — Charles Taylor convicted of aiding sexual slavery and use of child soldiers (2012)
cases.who: Charles Taylor, former President of Liberia; Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and allied rebel forces he aided
cases.what: On 26 April 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone, sitting in The Hague, convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor on all 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, on the basis of aiding and abetting crimes by the Revolutionary United Front during Sierra Leone's civil war, including sexual slavery and the recruitment and use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years in prison in May 2012.

cases.title: Sierra Leone — 29 Makeni children sent to US adopters without parents' consent (HANCI)
cases.who: Help A Needy Child International (HANCI)
cases.what: In 1998 about 29 children at HANCI's centre in Makeni were taken to Freetown for medical checks and never returned; parents later learned they had been adopted by Americans. Sierra Leone suspended adoptions on 21 May 2009. In April 2012 a presidential commission shut HANCI down and concluded the biological families 'cannot be said to have genuinely consented'.

cases.title: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation
cases.who: Aid workers (UN agencies, national and international NGOs), peacekeepers and community leaders
cases.what: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, including the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou; one substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated. OIOS (October 2002) found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of 'widespread' abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Sierra Leone — Truth and Reconciliation Commission: RUF and AFRC systematically abducted and raped girls aged 10 to 14 (2004)
cases.who: Revolutionary United Front (RUF), Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), Civil Defence Forces (CDF), Sierra Leone Army, West Side Boys
cases.what: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Sierra Leone released its final report in October 2004. It found that the RUF and the AFRC 'deliberately embarked on systematic strategies to abduct and rape women and girls between the ages of ten and 14 years', using them as sexual and domestic slaves and 'wives'; in a few cases the children were below ten. It also found that the CDF carried out a deliberate strategy of rape, sexual slavery and other sexual violations against girls, and that girls as young as 12 were forced to pay for aid with sex. Of 189 allegations of sexual slavery of women and girls reported to it, 72.5% were attributed to the RUF and 11.6% to the AFRC.

cases.title: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
cases.who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
cases.what: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.

flows.title: Freetown → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Freetown, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 56 in FY2003).

flows.title: Makeni → United States
flows.what: Children from the HANCI centre in Makeni adopted by Americans without genuine parental consent (presidential commission, 2012).

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2011: Sweden — Vanvårdsutredningen (SOU 2011:61).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2025: report: Swedish state inquiry report on intercountry adoption (2 June 2025)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 6,820 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (2% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
cases.who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
cases.what: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.

cases.title: Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989)
cases.who: Guatemalan armed forces and National Police; Secretaría de Bienestar Social (Hogar Elisa Martínez); notaries and courts
cases.what: In September 2009 the Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, part of the Peace Secretariat of the Presidency set up under President Álvaro Colom, published a study of adoptions during the internal armed conflict. It reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files recorded for 1977–1989 and found that the army and National Police transported children into the adoption system, that adoptions often rested on court declarations of abandonment with little effort to find parents, and that a 1977 decree let notaries formalise adoptions without a judge. Chief investigator Marco Tulio Álvarez told the press the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France.
cases.cover_up: Decree 54-77 (1977) let notaries complete adoptions without prior judicial approval; the welfare secretariat kept no record of how many children it received

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Europol: at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children missing in Europe (2016)
cases.who: Europol; organized crime exploiting the migrant flow
cases.what: On 31 January 2016 Europol's chief of staff Brian Donald told The Observer that at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy and 1,000 in Sweden, and that Europol had evidence some had been sexually exploited. He said an entire criminal infrastructure had developed over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow, with many arrests in Germany and Hungary. Save the Children estimated 26,000 unaccompanied children arrived in 2015.

cases.title: Swedish inquiry into abuse in children's homes and foster care (Vanvårdsutredningen)
cases.who: Swedish municipal children's homes and foster care
cases.what: The government inquiry into abuse and neglect in Swedish children's homes and foster care from 1920 to 1980 reported in February 2011, recommending a public apology and SEK 250,000 for each person who suffered serious abuse; the apology ceremony was held at Stockholm City Hall in 2011. A compensation board set up on 1 January 2013 had decided just over 4,000 applications by July 2015 and rejected 53% of them, with no right of appeal.

cases.title: Operation Atelier — network of abuse photographers
cases.who: Professional photographers producing abuse material
cases.what: Czech-initiated and supported by Europol and Eurojust: a Czech photographer exploited socially and financially disadvantaged children (close to 70) and, with a Swedish partner, distributed images to customers in the EU and Canada. In 2014 ten people were arrested in the Czech Republic (5), Sweden (2), France, Ireland and Spain; 30 TB of data were seized.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
cases.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
cases.what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

flows.title: Seoul → Sweden
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Sweden; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Colombo → Sweden
flows.what: Sri Lankan children adopted to Sweden in the 1980s (baby-farm period).

flows.title: Santiago → Sweden
flows.what: Children taken from Chilean mothers and adopted in Sweden, peaking under Pinochet; Sweden opened its own inquiry.

flows.title: Athens → Sweden
flows.what: Greek-born children adopted to Sweden 1950–1975; Greece restored their citizenship by law on 2 May 2025.

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Dreamboard
networks.what: Invitation-only board, about 600 members; 72 charged in Operation Delego (2011). Start year is approximate (investigation launched 2009).

networks.name: Boystown
networks.what: Tor platform with 400,000 registered users; four German administrators sentenced 7–12 years (2022).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.
Online network extorting minors into producing abuse material and self-harm; fragmented into subgroups (CVLT, 676, etc.) within 'The Com'.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found Middle East and North Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Canada → Rome: Fr Bernard Prince; Orán → Vatican: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta; Dominican Republic → Vatican: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.role_note: 2014: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child — concluding observations on the Holy See.
