patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, nuncio to the Dominican Republic (2013): Laicised 2014; Vatican trial on child-pornography charges announced June 2015; died 27 August 2015 before trial Msgr Carlo Alberto Capella, Holy See nunciature in Washington (2017): Convicted by a Vatican tribunal 2018: five years and a €5,000 fine — not tried in the US or Canada Archbishop Luigi Ventura, nuncio to France (2019): Tried in Paris in absentia; convicted 16 Dec 2020, eight-month suspended sentence Holy See and the Murphy Commission (Ireland) (2009): No Vatican files supplied Holy See and IICSA (England & Wales) (2020): — Vatican files and Poland's State Commission (2022): — Lateran concordat and Italian reporting (2012): —
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

cases.title: Vatican tribunal — diplomat Carlo Capella and the Martinelli trial
cases.who: Holy See diplomat Mgr Carlo Capella; St Pius X pre-seminary
cases.what: On 23 June 2018 the Vatican tribunal convicted Mgr Carlo Capella, recalled in 2017 from the Holy See's embassy in Washington, of possessing and sharing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years. In October 2020 the first Vatican criminal trial for sexual abuse began: Fr Gabriele Martinelli was accused of abusing an altar boy at the St Pius X pre-seminary inside the Vatican, and former rector Enrico Radice was charged with aiding and abetting.

cases.title: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Orán — convicted 2022
cases.who: Diocese of Orán; Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
cases.what: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned from the Diocese of Orán in August 2017, citing health, after complaints from clergy, and in December 2017 Pope Francis gave him a post created for him at the Vatican's patrimony office (APSA). Clergy had complained to the nunciature in 2015–2016 about his behaviour with seminarians and explicit images on his phone. On 4 March 2022 a court in Salta sentenced him to four and a half years for continued sexual abuse of two former seminarians, aggravated by his being a minister of religion. Included as a case of a bishop moved to the Vatican, though the victims were adults.
cases.cover_up: After resigning in 2017 amid complaints he was given a post at the Vatican's APSA in December 2017; suspended in January 2019

cases.title: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child — Holy See review (2014)
cases.who: Holy See
cases.what: On 5 February 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child said it was gravely concerned that the Holy See had not acknowledged the extent of the crimes, had not taken the necessary measures against child sexual abuse, and had adopted policies that allowed abuse to continue. It said the Holy See had consistently placed the church's reputation and the protection of perpetrators above children's best interests, accused it of transferring abusive priests to new parishes, urged it to require clergy to report abuse to police, and criticised a 'code of silence' under which whistleblowers were ostracised, demoted and fired.
cases.cover_up: Committee found abusive clergy were reassigned without police notification, bishops not required to report to civil authorities, and a code of silence

cases.title: McCarrick Report (Holy See, November 2020)
cases.who: Holy See; former Cardinal Theodore McCarrick
cases.what: The Holy See's report of 10 November 2020 found that Pope John Paul II appointed Theodore McCarrick Archbishop of Washington in 2000 despite a letter from Cardinal John O'Connor dated 28 October 1999 warning that the appointment would risk serious scandal, and after McCarrick denied the allegations. Benedict XVI did not order an investigation but had McCarrick told to retire in 2006 and keep a lower profile, which he did not do. The report said Francis did not learn that McCarrick was accused of abusing a minor until 2017. On 11 January 2019 the CDF found him guilty of solicitation in confession and sexual offences with minors and adults, and he was dismissed from the priesthood (announced 16 February 2019). A Massachusetts charge of assaulting a 16-year-old at a 1974 wedding reception was dismissed on 30 August 2023 after he was found incompetent to stand trial because of dementia. He died in April 2025.
cases.cover_up: A 1999 warning letter reached Pope John Paul II; an inquiry stalled after three of four US bishops gave 'inaccurate and incomplete information'; McCarrick was promoted to Washington in 2000

cases.title: Crimen sollicitationis — secrecy instruction (1962)
cases.who: Holy See — Holy Office (now Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith)
cases.what: The Holy Office instruction Crimen sollicitationis, approved by Pope John XXIII on 16 March 1962 and restating a 1922 instruction, governed canonical cases of solicitation in confession and also obscene acts with pre-adolescent children. It required absolute secrecy under pain of automatic excommunication. Many bishops did not know it was in their archives until press reports in 2003. Canon lawyer Thomas Doyle called the secrecy rules 'an explicit written policy to cover up cases', while others argue it did not bar reporting to police. It stayed in force until 2001.
cases.cover_up: Church proceedings to be kept absolutely confidential under automatic excommunication, binding tribunal members, accusers and witnesses

cases.title: Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela / De delictis gravioribus (2001)
cases.who: Holy See — Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, prefect)
cases.what: Pope John Paul II's motu proprio Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela (30 April 2001), with the CDF letter De delictis gravioribus of 18 May 2001 signed by its prefect Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, reserved to the CDF the delict of a cleric's sexual offence with a minor under 18, required bishops to notify the CDF after a preliminary investigation, and stated that such cases were subject to the pontifical secret, which remained until December 2019. In May 2014 the Holy See told the UN Committee against Torture that from 2004 to 2013 the CDF had studied 3,420 credible cases of abuse of minors and that 884 priests had been dismissed from the clerical state.
cases.cover_up: All abuse-of-minor cases reserved to the CDF under pontifical secret

cases.title: Pope Francis' letter to Chile's bishops and the Scicluna mission (2018)
cases.who: Pope Francis; Archbishop Charles Scicluna; Mgr Jordi Bertomeu
cases.what: After defending Bishop Juan Barros in January 2018, Pope Francis sent Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, who took 64 depositions in New York and Santiago; their report ran to more than 2,300 pages. In a letter of 8 April 2018 Francis wrote that he had 'made serious errors in the assessment and perception of the situation, in particular through the lack of reliable and balanced information', and summoned the Chilean bishops to Rome, where all of them offered to resign in May 2018.

cases.title: Vos estis lux mundi (2019) and February 2019 summit
cases.who: Pope Francis
cases.what: Three months after a February 2019 Vatican summit of bishops' conference presidents on abuse, Pope Francis issued Vos estis lux mundi, published on 9 May 2019. It requires clerics and religious to report suspected abuse and cover-ups promptly to church authorities, requires every diocese to set up a public reporting system, and lets bishops be investigated for abuse or cover-up. It applies 'without prejudice' to state reporting laws but does not itself require reporting to civil authorities. A revised permanent version was decreed on 25 March 2023 and took effect on 30 April 2023.

cases.title: Pontifical secret lifted for abuse cases (December 2019)
cases.who: Pope Francis
cases.what: On 17 December 2019 Pope Francis issued the instruction 'On the confidentiality of legal proceedings', removing the pontifical secret from cases of sexual abuse of minors and vulnerable persons, child abuse material and concealment of such crimes. Information must still be treated with 'security, integrity and confidentiality' but can be made available to state authorities, and church officials were told to comply with civil laws. In a separate change the same day, the age limit in the Vatican's definition of child abuse material was raised from 14 to 18.

cases.title: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions
cases.who: Salesians; Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo (Nobel Peace laureate)
cases.what: On 28 September 2022 Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Bishop Belo had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili, before and during his time as bishop. The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.
cases.cover_up: Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them until a magazine reported the case in 2022

cases.title: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
cases.who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
cases.what: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. A church tribunal found him guilty and the Vatican announced his laicisation on 27 June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic in 2008–2013 and for possessing child abuse images, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was arrested in Poland in February 2014; on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic (2009–2013) and two in Poland.
cases.cover_up: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic

flows.title: Canada → Rome: Fr Bernard Prince
flows.what: Prince was appointed to Rome in 1991; a 1993 church letter discussed keeping him hidden in the Vatican rather than facing justice in Canada.

flows.title: Orán → Vatican: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
flows.what: After resigning amid clergy complaints in 2017, Zanchetta was given a post at the Vatican's patrimony office in December 2017; he was convicted in Argentina in 2022 of abusing two adult seminarians.

flows.title: Dominican Republic → Vatican: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski
flows.what: The nuncio was recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; he was laicised in 2014 and died in 2015 before a Vatican trial.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Salesians of Don Bosco
networks.what: Order present in more than 130 countries. Documented cases include Boys' Town Sydney, the Don Rua juvenate in the Netherlands, US schools, Julian Fox (moved from Australia to Fiji in 1999), and Vatican sanctions on Salesian Bishop Belo of Timor-Leste.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: England → Zimbabwe (John Smyth 'exported to Africa').
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2022: Zimbabwe — Zimbabwe Gender Commission investigation into institutionalised sexual exploitation of girls and child marriages in apostolic sects (launched 24 Sept 2021; findings 2021–2023).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State schools and programmes where removed children were sexually abused
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Zimbabwe — sex trafficking around gold and diamond mines; girls traded under ngozi (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Zimbabwe — Gender Commission inquiry into sexual exploitation of girls and child marriage in apostolic sects (2021–2023)
cases.who: Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect and other apostolic church branches
cases.what: After a 14-year-old girl died in childbirth at a Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect shrine in August 2021, the Zimbabwe Gender Commission opened a public investigation on 24 September 2021 into sexual exploitation and abuse of girls and child marriages in apostolic sects. It identified compulsory virginity testing, wife pledging, betrothal and forced marriage in the Marange sect, and an earlier 2020 probe of branches around Marondera found girls of about 10 to 15 taken in as 'wives-in-waiting' and married at puberty. Its report for 2022 said it had received and investigated over 500 cases of child marriage and sexual exploitation and called for legislation regulating faith-based organisations.

cases.title: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
cases.who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
cases.what: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
cases.cover_up: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.

cases.title: Zimbabwe — sex trafficking around gold and diamond mines; girls traded under ngozi (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers at mining sites; families
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and children in sex trafficking around mines, sometimes for money or food, and may exploit children as panners and ore couriers in gold and diamond mines. Traditional practices including trading daughters for food or money and ngozi — giving a relative to another family to atone for a killing — make girls vulnerable. Low-level official complicity persisted.

flows.title: UK → Southern Rhodesia child migrants (Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College)
flows.what: IICSA found that children who told the headmaster they had been sexually abused by a padre at the college were beaten and warned against 'spreading malicious lies'; it lacked evidence to say whether Fairbridge UK knew of the allegations.

flows.title: England → Zimbabwe (John Smyth 'exported to Africa')
flows.what: After the 1982 Ruston Report on his beatings was kept from police, Smyth moved to Zimbabwe in 1984 and founded Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986. The Makin Review called him 'a problem solved and exported to Africa'.

flows.title: Zimbabwe → South Africa (John Smyth)
flows.what: Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, Smyth moved to South Africa in 2001, attending churches in Durban (from 2002) and Cape Town (Church on Main, 2004–2016). The Makin Review found it highly likely he kept abusing until his death in 2018.

networks.name: British child migration programmes
networks.what: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.

networks.name: Church of England
networks.what: IICSA counted 390 convicted offenders associated with the Church of England from the 1940s to 2018 and found a culture of deference and secrecy. The Peter Ball case and the Makin Review of John Smyth showed senior clergy withholding evidence; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.

networks.name: Anglican Communion (national Anglican churches)
networks.what: National Anglican churches with documented findings: Australia (1,082 complainants 1980–2015), Canada (residential schools; Nakayama), New Zealand (Dilworth School), and southern Africa (Smyth).
